findings.claim: Davidson's original compute-centric takeoff model (2023) defines an 'effective FLOP gap' -- the multiplier on training compute needed to go from AI that can automate 20% of cognitive tasks to AGI (100%) -- and estimates it at 10,000x, with wide uncertainty.
findings.author: Tom Davidson (Open Philanthropy)

findings.claim: Davidson's Full Takeoff Model (interactive playground at takeoffspeeds.com) has a slider parameter called 'R&D parallelization penalty' whose preset best-guess value, per an external review, is 0.7 on the playground's scale (the reviewer argued this should be far higher based on Besiroglu et al. duplication-of-labor estimates of ~0.02-0.13% returns).
findings.author: review of Davidson's takeoff model (LessWrong, 2023)

findings.claim: Davidson's takeoff model uses a 'returns to software R&D' parameter: each doubling of cumulative software R&D spending drives approximately 1.25 doublings of software efficiency.
findings.author: review of Davidson's takeoff model (LessWrong, 2023)

findings.claim: Davidson's 2023 model designates 20% automation of cognitive tasks (weighted by 2020 output share) as the key milestone ('20%-AI'), and asks how long it takes to go from 20%-AI to 100%-AI ('takeoff duration'); Monte Carlo median AGI date ~2043-2045 with median takeoff duration ~3-3.6 years.
findings.author: Tom Davidson

findings.claim: GATE (Epoch AI's Growth and AI Transition Endogenous model) parameterizes task bottlenecking with a CES 'substitution parameter' rho < 0 across tasks; default central estimate rho = -0.65, producing large near-term growth accelerations.
findings.author: Epoch AI

findings.claim: GATE's automation-fraction -> growth-rate mapping (from Epoch's own simulation): even 30% task automation can push growth rates above 20%/year; 'explosive growth' (>30%/yr, the classic threshold) requires roughly 50-70% of tasks automated; at 40% automation GATE predicts ~12% GWP growth.
findings.author: Epoch AI

findings.claim: GATE combines a compute-to-capability module (extensive margin: fraction of tasks automatable; intensive margin: efficiency per task, i.e. 'digital worker' count) with a semi-endogenous growth model; conservative hardware/software return assumptions imply full task automation is reachable within ~20 years, with automation eventually enabling 30-100% annual GDP growth.
findings.author: Epoch AI

findings.claim: AI-2027's 'Superhuman Coder' (SC) milestone is explicitly defined via a compute/parallelism multiplier: an AI system that a lab could run, using 5% of its compute budget, as 30x as many agent-copies as it has human researchers, each coding at 30x human speed.
findings.author: Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland, Romeo Dean (AI Futures Project)

findings.claim: AI-2027 assigns explicit 'AI R&D progress multiplier' values at each of four capability milestones: Superhuman Coder (SC) 5x, Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) 25x, Superintelligent AI Researcher (SIAR) 250x, Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) 2,000x algorithmic-progress speedup relative to unaided human researchers.
findings.author: Daniel Kokotajlo et al. (AI Futures Project)

findings.claim: AI-2027's concrete 2027 deployment scenario: at Superhuman Coder milestone with ~10 million H100-equivalents, 5% compute allocation to inference yields 200,000 parallel AI researcher copies, equivalent to 50,000 agents at 30x human task speed (each processing ~400 tokens/second).
findings.author: Daniel Kokotajlo et al. (AI Futures Project)

findings.claim: AI-2027 estimates 'human-only' (no AI assistance) time gaps between milestones -- SC to SAR: 4 years median (80% CI 1.5-10y); SAR to SIAR: 19 years median (80% CI 2.3-380y); SIAR to ASI: 95 years median (80% CI 2.4-1,000,000y) -- versus actual (AI-assisted) forecast gaps of 0.3y, 0.3y, and 0.16y respectively, i.e. the R&D-speedup multipliers compress each gap roughly 10-600x.
findings.author: Daniel Kokotajlo et al. (AI Futures Project)

findings.claim: Davidson, Halperin, Houlden & Korinek (NBER WP 35155, April 2026) give an explicit closed-form CES/Cobb-Douglas 'explosion condition' for algorithmic progress: growth becomes hyperbolic (finite-time singularity) iff f_Y + f_S(1/beta_S) + f_H(1/beta_H) + f_A(1/(1-alpha))(1/beta_A) > 1, where f_i is the AI-automated task share in sector i (Y=output, S=software, H=hardware, A=general TFP/ideas) and beta_i is the degree of diminishing returns to research in that sector.
findings.author: Tom Davidson, Basil Halperin, Thomas Houlden, Anton Korinek

findings.claim: The NBER paper's central calibration table (Table 3): labor share in production 1-alpha = 0.6; returns-to-research parameter r_S (software) ≈ 1 (from Erdil, Besiroglu & Ho 2024, chess-engine data); r_H (hardware) = 5 (from Bloom et al. 2020); r_A (aggregate TFP) = 0.32 (from Bloom et al. 2020, i.e. beta_A = 3.1 'ideas getting harder to find' economy-wide, with hardware showing the least diminishing returns at beta_H = 0.2).
findings.author: Tom Davidson, Basil Halperin, Thomas Houlden, Anton Korinek

findings.claim: The NBER paper's headline quantitative result: automating research uniformly across all four sectors (software, hardware, general TFP, final-goods production) requires only 13% task automation to cross the hyperbolic-growth threshold; automating only software+hardware research requires 17%; hardware automation alone requires 20%; fully automating software research alone (with ~0% elsewhere) sits almost exactly at the knife-edge threshold (EC=1.00).
findings.author: Tom Davidson, Basil Halperin, Thomas Houlden, Anton Korinek

findings.claim: The NBER paper's simulation: starting from a balanced growth path and calibrating to Epoch AI (2026)'s measured 2026 growth rates of software efficiency (110%/yr) and hardware efficiency (37%/yr), a one-time automation shock of full software-R&D automation (f_S=1) plus just 5% automation elsewhere is enough to cross the explosive threshold and produces a finite-time 'singularity' within roughly six years; a uniform 13% automation shock across all sectors is the double-exponential knife-edge, with 15%/20% uniform automation producing singularities in ~16/~9 years respectively.
findings.author: Tom Davidson, Basil Halperin, Thomas Houlden, Anton Korinek

findings.claim: The NBER paper's formal CES generalization for bottlenecks (Section 6): effective labor in each sector is a CES aggregate of human labor L and AI labor C with parameter theta<1 (theta->1 recovers Cobb-Douglas/no-bottleneck); the AI-elasticity of effective labor is eta_i = 1/(1 + x_i^(1/theta) (C_i/L_i)^((1-theta)/theta)) where x_i=(1-f_i)/f_i, and eta_i -> 0 as C_i/L_i -> infinity for any theta<1, i.e. bottlenecks generically prevent a singularity unless automation share f_i -> 1.
findings.author: Tom Davidson, Basil Halperin, Thomas Houlden, Anton Korinek

findings.claim: Erdil & Besiroglu's task-based CES growth model (predecessor to GATE) finds that whether automation produces 'explosive' growth depends critically on the CES substitution parameter rho across tasks: rho=-1 implies output could increase ~100-fold (very likely explosive unless spread over much longer than a decade), whereas blocking massive output increases requires rho below about -2, which the authors consider implausibly strong complementarity (stronger than currently believed to hold between capital and labor).
findings.author: Ege Erdil (and Tamay Besiroglu), Epoch AI

findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt

findings.claim: Indifference-based definition of 'speedup': the multiplier on your own working speed that would make you indifferent to having the AI tools instead
findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt

findings.claim: Overall AI-progress speedup is much smaller than the serial engineering speedup because engineering speedup must be discounted through several compounding factors
findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt

findings.claim: Algorithmic progress's share of overall AI progress (the rest being driven by scaling training compute and data spend)
findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt

findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt

findings.claim: Anthropic leadership also cite a looser ~90%+ figure for code including scripts and experimental (non-production) code
findings.author: Anthropic leadership (paraphrase in institute post)

findings.author: Anthropic

findings.claim: Anthropic internal poll (March 2026, n=130 employees): median self-reported ~4x output multiplier from access to 'Mythos Preview' (an internal-only more capable model) vs. no AI access
findings.author: Anthropic (internal employee poll, n=130)

findings.claim: Anthropic AI R&D capability evals: Claude Opus 4.6 achieved 427x speedup on a kernel-optimization eval using a novel scaffold, exceeding the 300x threshold used to rule out AI R&D-4

findings.claim: Anthropic Opus 4.6 System Card: internal survey of intensive users reported wide range of self-estimated productivity uplift, mean 152%, median 100% (i.e., 'twice as productive' on average by mean, or 'doubled' by median)
findings.author: Anthropic, Claude Opus 4.6 System Card (internal survey of Claude Code power users)

findings.claim: Anthropic Opus 4.5 System Card: internal survey of 18 intensive Claude Code users -- 9 of 18 reported >=100% productivity improvement (i.e., work at least doubled); median 100%, mean 220%; none believed the model could fully automate an entry-level remote-only research/engineering role
findings.author: Anthropic, Claude Opus 4.5 System Card

findings.claim: Anthropic Opus 4.5 System Card: model's autonomous research judgment matched/exceeded human researcher choices in a comparison exercise
findings.author: Anthropic

findings.claim: Anthropic institute post: autonomous Claude agents recovered 97% of a performance gap over 800 cumulative hours using $18,000 of compute, vs. two human researchers recovering ~23% of the same gap in about a week

findings.author: Anthropic

findings.author: Boris Cherny (Anthropic) and unnamed Anthropic spokesperson, via Fortune

findings.claim: Dario Amodei (Anthropic CEO), Council on Foreign Relations, March 2025: predicted AI would write 90% of code within 3-6 months, ~100% within 12 months
findings.author: Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, remarks at Council on Foreign Relations

findings.claim: Redwood Research independent/skeptical reconstruction: Anthropic company-wide AI-authored-merged-code share was closer to ~50% (not 90%) as of late 2025, and the true productivity multiplier from AI is 'much less than 10x, probably less than 2x'

findings.claim: Anthropic AI R&D capability threshold determinations (safety framework): Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 both assessed as NOT crossing the 'AI R&D-4' autonomous-research capability threshold, though some Opus 4.6 survey respondents believed it might already qualify with sufficiently powerful scaffolding
findings.author: Anthropic, Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 System Cards

findings.claim: Google: share of new code at Google that is AI-generated rose from >25% (Oct 2024) to >30% (Apr 2025) to ~50% (late 2025) to 75% (Apr 2026), per CEO Sundar Pichai on quarterly earnings calls
findings.author: Sundar Pichai, CEO, Alphabet/Google, quarterly earnings calls

findings.claim: Google DeepMind AlphaEvolve: in production for over a year, continuously recovers on average 0.7% of Google's worldwide compute resources via a data-center job-scheduling algorithm redesign
findings.author: Google DeepMind (official blog)

findings.claim: AlphaEvolve sped up a key kernel in Gemini's architecture by 23%, yielding a 1% reduction in Gemini's overall training time; compressed kernel-optimization engineering effort from 'weeks of expert effort to days of automated experiments'
findings.author: Google DeepMind

findings.claim: AlphaEvolve achieved up to a 32.5% speedup for the FlashAttention kernel implementation used in Transformer-based AI models, and found a Verilog circuit simplification adopted into an upcoming Google TPU
findings.author: Google DeepMind

findings.claim: AlphaEvolve mathematical/algorithmic discovery hit-rate across a broad internal problem set: rediscovered SOTA in ~75% of cases and improved on SOTA in ~20% of cases
findings.author: Google DeepMind

findings.claim: OpenAI: internal employee usage of Codex agents rose from ~40% (Aug 2025) to 97.9% of employees (as of ~June 2026); average worker spent <10% of tokens on Codex through Aug 2025, rising to near-total reliance by mid-2026
findings.author: OpenAI ('How agents are transforming work' / accompanying research paper 'The Shift to Agentic AI: Evidence from Codex'), reported by The Register

findings.claim: OpenAI: non-developer (e.g., legal, recruiting, finance) usage of Codex rose sharply; legal/recruiting crossed to majority-Codex use around April 2026; average OpenAI lawyer/recruiter now generates >85% of output tokens via Codex; legal team's monthly output tokens (Codex+ChatGPT) 13x higher in June 2026 vs Nov 2025
findings.author: OpenAI, reported by The Register

findings.claim: OpenAI: share of individual Codex users submitting at least one task estimated to take an experienced human >8 hours rose nearly 10x since the start of 2026
findings.author: OpenAI, reported by The Register

findings.claim: Roon (pseudonymous OpenAI researcher, X/Twitter): reports writing 0% of own code personally ('100%, I don't write code anymore')
findings.author: Roon, OpenAI researcher (pseudonymous X account), via Fortune

findings.author: Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, World Economic Forum Davos panel

findings.claim: Original METR time-horizon paper: 50%-reliability time horizon has been doubling approximately every 7 months since 2019.
findings.author: METR (Kwa, West, Barnes et al.)

findings.claim: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 50% time horizon at TH1.0 release (March 2025).
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: 80%-reliability time horizons are roughly 5x shorter than 50%-reliability horizons, but have a similar doubling time.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: Time horizon varies hugely by domain; agentic computer-use tasks lag far behind software/reasoning tasks.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: METR's RCT found that allowing experienced open-source developers to use early-2025 AI tools (Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) made them 19% SLOWER on real tasks in mature codebases, despite the same models having ~1-hour time horizons -- directly relevant to reconciling time-horizon trend with real R&D uplift.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: METR's own explanation for the gap between rising time horizons (implying strong capability) and the measured 19% RCT slowdown: 'algorithmic' benchmark scoring (does the code pass tests) overstates real usability because it ignores the large amount of surrounding work (tests, docs, lint, review, integration) needed to make AI output mergeable.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: METR explicitly states that doubling the time horizon does NOT double the degree of task automation / real-world uplift, because of nonlinear failure modes and because time horizon measures serial human-labor replacement, not autonomous operation length.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: METR flags severe task-distribution and selection-bias caveats: benchmark tasks are deliberately chosen to be near the frontier of current capability, are self-contained/low-context/well-defined, and don't require the collaboration or context-accumulation that most real months-long projects need.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: Time Horizon 1.1 (Jan 2026 methodology update): expanded and re-curated task suite, producing tighter estimates especially at longer horizons, and revising the doubling-time trend upward (faster) for the post-2023 period.
findings.author: METR (@METR_Evals)

findings.claim: Time Horizon 1.1 current 50%-horizon estimates for top models (as of the Jan 2026 update / its data as fetched mid-2026).
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: Greenblatt's mid-2026 read of the frontier: 50%-reliability METR benchmark has effectively saturated (too easy to be a reliable discriminator among top models); the live signal is now the 80%-reliability horizon, where public models lag internal/frontier-lab-internal models.
findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt (Redwood Research)

findings.claim: Independent tracking (LessWrong/Substack analysis, Feb 2026) of the TH1.1 update: the rate of frontier time-horizon growth increased to ~10x/year (about every 3.5 months) for the most recent period, up from ~3x/year (~7 month doubling) pre-2024.
findings.author: John C (LessWrong/Read the OOM, third-party analysis of METR data)

findings.claim: METR's own TH1.1 update quantifies the doubling-time trend across three windows, showing acceleration over time.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: Headline result: AI tool access caused a 19% INCREASE in task completion time (slowdown), not a speedup, for experienced open-source developers on their own mature repos.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Perceived vs actual gap: developers forecast AI would speed them up before the study, still believed they had been sped up afterward, despite actually being slowed down.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: External expert forecasters (ML researchers and economists) overestimated AI speedup even more than the developers themselves.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Exact RCT design and sample.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Developer and repository characteristics: highly experienced developers, large/mature high-quality codebases.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: AI tools/models used were Feb-June 2025 frontier tools, primarily Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet; developers had substantial general LLM experience but limited experience with this specific tool.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: The paper's own headline finding on the perception/behavior mechanism: when using AI, developers shift time away from active coding/searching toward reviewing AI output, prompting, waiting on AI, and idling.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Authors' own list of factors that could explain non-generalization to other settings (e.g. frontier labs, less mature codebases) -- factors found LIKELY to contribute to slowdown in this specific study.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Authors' explicit Key Caveats section: results should NOT be over-generalized because the two main drivers (developer familiarity, repo size/maturity) are specific to this setting.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Authors' second caveat: current tool/model limitations (latency, reliability, elicitation) may not persist; better scaffolding, more inference compute, or domain fine-tuning could produce positive speedup in this same setting.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Authors' third caveat / most direct 'lab response'-relevant finding: preliminary (forthcoming at publication) evidence that fully autonomous AI agents (not just IDE-copilot-style assistance) can often correctly implement the core functionality of these same repositories' issues, though failing on secondary requirements.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: Study explicitly distinguishes itself from prior literature that found speedups, attributing the difference to task realism, fixed (pre-registered) outcome measures, and using genuinely experienced developers on their own high-standard codebases.
findings.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)

findings.claim: METR follow-up: a larger, late-2025 attempted replication with more developers and newer AI tools was compromised by severe selection effects and abandoned/redesigned rather than yielding a clean updated estimate.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: METR follow-up quote illustrating the selection-effect mechanism: developers increasingly did not want to be randomized away from AI access.
findings.author: METR (quoting a study participant)

findings.claim: Other RCT: GitHub Copilot controlled experiment -- large, statistically strong speedup on a synthetic/self-contained coding task.
findings.author: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer (Microsoft/GitHub)

findings.claim: Other RCT: Google-internal enterprise RCT on real internal codebase task -- moderate speedup, NOT statistically significant at conventional threshold.
findings.author: Elise Paradis, Kate Grey, Quinn Madison, Daye Nam, Andrew Macvean, Nan Zhang, Ben Ferrari-Church, Satish Chandra (Google)

findings.claim: Greenblatt's central Amdahl-style datapoint: current AI-driven engineering speedup at frontier labs (~1.6x) is much larger than the resulting overall AI progress speedup (~1.15-1.2x), because engineering labor is only one input among several that don't speed up as much.
findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt (Redwood Research)

findings.claim: Greenblatt: AI-written code in current frontier AI R&D is 'sloppier, less reliable, and less well understood' than human-written code, creating an understanding/verification gap, though this is often tolerable because R&D projects are small and self-contained.
findings.author: Ryan Greenblatt (Redwood Research)

findings.claim: Industry survey (Sonar 'State of Code' 2026): developers do not fully trust AI-generated code and often skip review despite this, and a substantial minority say AI-code review is *more* effortful than reviewing human code -- direct proxy for a 'verification tax' on AI-written code.
findings.author: Sonar (SonarSource), 'State of Code' developer survey

findings.claim: METR's RCT: giving experienced open-source developers early-2025 AI coding tools made them 19% SLOWER on real tasks in mature codebases -- attributed substantially to time spent reviewing/correcting AI output -- despite developers believing (both before and after) that AI had sped them up.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: METR's simplified AI-timelines model formally applies Amdahl's law to AI R&D automation: once fraction f of tasks is automated (and automated tasks are much faster than manual ones), overall speedup is capped at 1/(1-f), so un-automated/serial tasks dominate wall-clock time as f rises.
findings.author: Thomas Kwa / METR

findings.claim: Epoch AI: final training runs are only a small fraction of total AI R&D compute spending at three frontier-ish labs -- most compute goes to the many smaller experiments, ablations, and failed runs that precede a final training run -- and R&D/experiment workloads have lower GPU utilization than final runs due to overhead (waiting between runs, failed jobs, debugging, idle time).
findings.author: Ben Denain & Yafah Edelman / Epoch AI

findings.claim: Epoch AI: training run durations are structurally capped in practice (rarely exceeding ~6 months), and further scaling faces a compute-scale ceiling around 2e28 FLOP if runs must stay under ~3 months, because data-movement time begins to dominate arithmetic time -- i.e. training itself has a hard wall-clock floor that automation of coding/labor cannot shrink.
findings.author: Epoch AI

findings.claim: Sholto Douglas (then Google DeepMind, now Anthropic): writing code is 'a small fraction of the job' in frontier ML research; labs are 'somewhat compute bound' with 'always more experiments you could run'; the actual bottlenecks are interpreting/understanding experimental results and research 'taste' (prioritization under uncertainty), not code volume.
findings.author: Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken, interviewed by Dwarkesh Patel

findings.claim: Survey of 25 frontier-lab researchers/forecasters on automating AI R&D: multiple participants independently identify human oversight/approval and 'research taste'/idea-evaluation as the bottlenecks that persist after coding is automated, and expect the org to actively try to remove the human bottleneck.
findings.author: survey of AI researchers/forecasters (arXiv 2603.03338)

findings.claim: Tom Davidson / Forethought formal model of a software intelligence explosion: training-run duration and experiment-compute availability are the two candidate hard serial bottlenecks that could cap a software-only intelligence explosion even with unlimited automated research labor; the model's central parameter is r (returns to software R&D), with r>1 required for an explosion.
findings.author: Tom Davidson / Forethought (related formal writeup: Whitfill & Wu, arXiv:2507.23181)

findings.claim: Epoch/Davidson-style compute-bottleneck argument: training compute is enormously more scarce than inference compute, so a fully-automated research workforce running on 'saved' inference compute is not itself compute-constrained the way training/experimentation is -- but experiment throughput (not final-model inference) is the actual bottleneck once coding is automated.
findings.author: Tom Davidson / Forethought

findings.claim: Institutional/decision-latency bottleneck: rigid social, political, and organizational decision-making schedules act as a serial bottleneck on AI-accelerated progress because these processes cannot themselves be sped up by faster AI cognition -- 'accelerating technological progress is like slowing the processes which don't accelerate along with it.'
findings.author: Will MacAskill & Fin Moorhouse / Forethought

findings.claim: Amodei's 'Machines of Loving Grace' analogy: even a fully competent virtual biologist/researcher is bottlenecked by the physical, serial nature of real-world experimentation (running assays, waiting for biological/clinical timelines) unless AI also helps redesign the experimental paradigm itself (e.g. in-vitro proxies for in-vivo, faster instruments, regulatory/trial reform).
findings.author: Dario Amodei (Anthropic)

findings.claim: Epoch's 'Toward an O*NET for AI R&D' piece does not contain any time-use percentages, importance weights, or empirical data on how researchers/engineers allocate time across the 6 categories or 62 tasks -- it is purely a taxonomy proposal, not a time-use study.
findings.author: Epoch AI

findings.claim: General software developers spend well under half their workweek writing/improving code; the remainder splits across code maintenance, testing, security, and meetings/operational work. Role matters: pure developers spend more time coding than DevOps/managers.
findings.author: Sonar (SonarSource), State of Code Developer Survey

findings.claim: Developers report spending a large minority of their week on technical debt/maintenance rather than new code/features -- an independent, earlier data point corroborating the Sonar split.
findings.author: Stripe, 'The Developer Coefficient'

findings.claim: Knowledge workers broadly (not developer-specific) report spending the majority of their time on coordination overhead rather than skilled or strategic work.
findings.author: Asana, Anatomy of Work Index

findings.claim: In Anthropic's internal August 2025 survey of engineers/researchers, Claude usage grew sharply and its use-mix shifted from low-level coding tasks toward higher-level design/planning and larger feature work -- a proxy for how the underlying human work composition is (or isn't) changing.
findings.author: Anthropic

findings.claim: Anthropic engineers self-report a qualitative shift in role composition toward reviewing/revising AI output rather than authoring code from scratch.
findings.author: Anthropic

findings.claim: Across the general Claude.ai + API traffic (not lab-internal), Computer & Mathematical / programming-type tasks are the single largest occupational task cluster, and are especially concentrated in programmatic (API) use, consistent with 'Build' work dominating automatable task-mix for technical roles.
findings.author: Anthropic Economic Index

findings.claim: METR's early-2025 RCT on experienced open-source developers measured time at ~10-second resolution via 143 hours of manually-labeled screen recordings (29% of total study hours), but METR's public writeup reports only the AI-vs-no-AI time delta (AI made developers 19% slower), not a full activity-category breakdown (coding vs. testing vs. planning vs. review) for the general workday.
findings.author: METR

findings.claim: Research-engineer (RE) and research-scientist (RS) roles at frontier labs are described in job postings and hiring guides as differing in primary orientation -- RE toward implementation/scaling/infrastructure, RS toward novel methods/experimentation/publication -- but the boundary is explicitly described as blurred at Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind, i.e. there is no clean, stable time-use split by title.
findings.author: Sundeep Teki (AI Research Engineer/Scientist interview guides, drawing on public lab career pages)
